### Part 1
(30 points)

There is a planet orbiting [Proxima Centauri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proxima_Centauri) that has a population of organisms which are very human-like.
As it happens, a group within the larger population uses a system a lot like Arabic numeral arithmetic to perform arithmetic calculations, except that the syntax and semantics are slightly different.
This group uses a base-7 number system, and the atomic numerals have different meanings than they do in Arabic numeral arithmetic.
We can call the language they use for arithmetic calculations $L_{NANA}$ (not Arabic numeral arithmetic).

To be more precise, for this group within the population which lives on the planet orbiting Proxima Centauri, the set of *atomic* numerals is the following one:

$$atom = \{⌜1⌝, ⌜2⌝, ⌜3⌝, ⌜4⌝, ⌜5⌝, ⌜6⌝, ⌜7⌝\}$$

Meanwhile, the interpretation function of the model employed by this group, $I_{NANA}$, is the following one:

$$I_{NANA}(⌜1⌝) = 6$$
$$I_{NANA}(⌜2⌝) = 5$$
$$I_{NANA}(⌜3⌝) = 4$$
$$I_{NANA}(⌜4⌝) = 3$$
$$I_{NANA}(⌜5⌝) = 2$$
$$I_{NANA}(⌜6⌝) = 1$$
$$I_{NANA}(⌜7⌝) = 0$$

The full model of $L_{NANA}$ employed by this group is thus:

$$\mathcal{M}_{NANA} = ⟨ℕ, \{\True, \False\}, I_{NANA}⟩$$

One more thing.
These guys use the following modification of the numeral concatenation rule (Rule 2) which we defined in [Arabic numeral arithmetic: semantics](ana_semantics.html):

\begin{prooftree}
\AxiomC{$⟨x, ⟦x⟧_{\mathcal{M}_{NANA}}⟩ ⊢ n$}
\AxiomC{$⟨y, ⟦y⟧_{\mathcal{M}_{NANA}}⟩ ⊢ n$}
\RightLabel{Rule 2}\BinaryInfC{$⟨x^{⌢}y, ⟦x⟧_{\mathcal{M}_{NANA}} * 7^{length(y)} + ⟦y⟧_{\mathcal{M}_{NANA}}⟩ ⊢ n$}
\end{prooftree}

The rules for generating strings of $L_{NANA}$ and their interpretations are otherwise identical to those for generating strings of $L_{ANA}$ and their interpretations.

Show that $⌜((53 + 6) × 5) = 24⌝$ is a sentence (i.e., an $s$) of $L_{NANA}$, and show what its interpretation in $\mathcal{M}_{NANA}$ is.

### Part 2
(35 points)

Consider the sentence in (@ex-bo).

(@ex-bo) Bo jumps without running.

Assume (contra actual fact) that the word *without* is a connective, like *and*.
Assume also that *running* is a $vp$ with the same meaning as *runs*.
Provide a lexical entry for *without*, and use it---along with the grammar fragment defined in [A first approximation of English](english.html) and the model defined in [An English model and example](english_examples.html)---to give a derivation of (@ex-bo).
Note that you are effectively modifying the model's interpretation function (as well as the alphabet $\Sigma_{\textit{Eng.}}$) by adding two new words.

### Part 3
(35 points)

As you know, English does not only have sentences in which *and* coordinates two verb phrases.
It *also* has sentences like (@ex-bo-two-clauses).

(@ex-bo-two-clauses) Bo jumps and Bo runs.

Let us assume that in addition to the word *and*, English has another word, *and2*, which is *pronounced* exactly the same way as *and* is pronounced (i.e., /ænd/), but which coordinates *sentences* instead of verb phrases.
Thus *and* is the variant of the coordinator that appears earlier in the notes, while *and2* is the variant of the coordinator that appears in (@ex-bo-two-clauses).

Provide a lexical entry for the variant of the coordinator which appears in (@ex-bo-two-clauses)---something that can be added to the lexicon given in [A first approximation of English](english.html).
Add another rule, as well---a "Rule 3"---and a new syntactic category (if you need to) that lets you derive (@ex-bo-two-clauses) as an $s$.
Give a derivation showing that (@ex-bo-two-clauses) is a sentence with a meaning, using this lexical entry.
Does your lexical entry ensure that (@ex-bo-two-clauses) and (@ex-bo2) entail each other (regardless of the particular meanings of $\textit{Bo}$, $\textit{jumps}$, and $\textit{runs}$)?

(@ex-bo2) Bo jumps and runs.

If so, how does it ensure this?
